lessons.title: Market mindset and what moves price
objectives: Separate opinion from a testable trade plan
Understand that price reacts to flow, sentiment, and expectations

objective_notes.Separate opinion from a testable trade p:
Opinion = "I believe this stock should go up."

Testable trade plan = "I will buy if it breaks above $50 on higher-than-average volume, risking no more than 2% of my capital, and I will exit the position if it falls below $47."
objective_notes.Understand that price reacts to flow, se: Capital flows, institutional positioning, and changes in market sentiment can move prices long before fundamentals fully reflect those changes. Markets are forward-looking, so prices often respond more to expectations about future earnings, growth, and risk than to current results.

sections.heading: What moves the market
sections.body: Prices change when buyers and sellers disagree on value and when capital rotates between assets. Macro conditions set the backdrop; order flow and positioning drive day-to-day moves. Bullish investors (bulls) push prices higher when they expect future gains, while bearish investors (bears) create selling pressure when they anticipate weaker performance or increased risk.

sections.heading: Professional habits
sections.body: Define thesis, invalidation, maximum loss, and time horizon before entry. Look for clean setups rather than forcing trades in unclear conditions.

key_points: The market does not owe you a move in your direction
Bid is the highest price buyers are willing to pay; ask is the lowest price sellers are willing to accept.

Liquidity and spread matter as much as direction. Highly liquid markets generally allow traders to enter and exit positions more easily and at lower cost, while wide bid-ask spreads can significantly reduce profits and increase trading risk, especially in volatile conditions.
lessons.practice: Write one sentence each for thesis, stop/invalidation, and target before any trade.

lessons.title: Support, resistance, and structure
objectives: Identify areas where supply and demand historically concentrated

sections.heading: Support and resistance
sections.body: Support is a zone where buying has repeatedly appeared. Resistance is where selling has repeatedly capped advances. Levels are zones, not exact prices.

sections.heading: Retracements
sections.body: Trends rarely move in straight lines. Pullbacks to prior structure or moving averages are common places to reassess risk versus reward.

key_points: Broken resistance can become support (and vice versa). Once a resistance level is decisively broken, it often acts as a support zone as buyers step in to defend the new price level; the opposite can occur when support is broken.

Retracements are a normal part of healthy trends. Temporary pullbacks allow the market to digest gains or losses, reset sentiment, and create new opportunities for entries with better risk-to-reward ratios.
Volume helps validate retracements. A pullback on declining volume is often less concerning than one accompanied by heavy selling pressure, which may signal a deeper reversal.
Moving averages can act as dynamic support or resistance. Many traders monitor key averages such as the 20-, 50-, or 200-period moving average to identify areas where trends may resume.
lessons.practice: Mark three levels on a daily chart of your active symbol and note what happened at each.

lessons.title: Candlestick context
objectives: Understand how each candle summarizes the battle between buyers and sellers during a specific period, showing the open, high, low, and close prices.
Learn to identify who was in control of the market and how that control may be changing over time.

Read candles as evidence of control, not as guaranteed signals. A candle reflects what happened during a period of trading, providing clues about market psychology and momentum, but it does not predict the future with certainty.

sections.heading: Useful patterns
sections.body: Narrow range bars suggest consolidation. Wide range bars show decisive participation. Topping or bottoming tails can show rejection at a level. Change-of-character bars may hint at a shift in control when they appear after a trend.

sections.heading: Caution
sections.body: Patterns work best with location (near support/resistance) and volume confirmation—not in isolation.

key_points: Context beats pattern names
lessons.practice: Find one wide-range bar and one narrow-range bar on your symbol and describe who won that session.

lessons.title: Volume and gaps
objectives: Use volume to judge conviction behind a move

sections.heading: Volume
sections.body: Rising price on strong volume suggests participation. Rising price on weak volume can be fragile. Distribution often shows as heavy volume on down days.

sections.heading: Gaps
sections.body: Gaps mark imbalance between sessions. They can act as magnets (fill) or acceleration points depending on context and follow-through.

key_points: Volume confirms; it does not predict alone
lessons.practice: Compare up-day versus down-day volume on the last ten sessions.

lessons.title: Trend and multiple time frames
objectives: Align shorter-term trades with higher-time-frame bias when possible

sections.heading: Trend analysis
sections.body: Higher highs and higher lows define uptrends; the opposite defines downtrends. Trade with the dominant trend unless you have a specific mean-reversion plan.

sections.heading: Multiple time frames
sections.body: Use a higher frame for bias (weekly/daily) and a lower frame for entries (daily/intraday). Conflicting frames increase whipsaw risk.

sections.heading: Moving averages
sections.body: Moving averages smooth price. They are tools for context—dynamic support/resistance—not magic lines.

key_points: One time frame for direction, one for timing
lessons.practice: State the daily trend and whether your intended hold period matches it.

lessons.title: Market internals
objectives: Gauge broad market health beyond a single stock

sections.heading: Common tools
sections.body: Equity put/call ratio, VIX (implied volatility of index options), TICK (NYSE uptick minus downtick), and TRIN (arms index) help describe risk appetite and breadth.

sections.heading: Relative strength
sections.body: A stock outperforming its sector or index may deserve long bias; underperformance may favor caution or hedging.

key_points: Internals describe regime; they do not replace stock-level analysis
lessons.practice: Note whether VIX is rising or falling this week and what that implies for option premium.

lessons.title: Money management
objectives: Size positions so a normal loss does not impair decision-making

sections.heading: After losing streaks
sections.body: Reduce size, pause new strategies, and return to checklist discipline. Revenge trading magnifies drawdowns.

sections.heading: Position sizing
sections.body: Risk a small, fixed fraction of capital per idea. Define maximum loss before entry, including commissions.

key_points: Survival first, optimization second
lessons.practice: Calculate dollar risk if your stop is hit on your next stock trade.

lessons.title: Calls and puts
objectives: Know rights, obligations, and contract multiplier

sections.heading: Definitions
sections.body: A call gives the buyer the right to buy the underlying at the strike before expiration. A put gives the right to sell. Sellers take the opposite obligation.

sections.heading: Contract multiplier
sections.body: One standard equity option contract typically represents 100 shares. A premium of $3.00 per share is $300 per contract before fees.

key_points: Buy options: limited risk to premium (long). Sell options: obligation risk can be large
lessons.practice: Use the Options P&L simulator with one call and one put at the same strike.

lessons.title: Expiration calendar
objectives: Choose expiration that matches your thesis timeline

sections.heading: Monthly options
sections.body: Standard monthly contracts usually expire on the third Friday of the month (Thursday if Friday is a holiday).

sections.heading: Weeklies and 0DTE
sections.body: Weekly expirations exist on many liquid names. Some index products have daily expirations for short-term trading—theta decay is extreme.

sections.heading: LEAPS
sections.body: Long-dated options (often nine months or more) behave like stock substitutes with less capital than buying shares outright.

key_points: More time costs more premium but forgives timing errors better
lessons.practice: Set days to expiration in the simulator and move 'days elapsed' to see theta effect.

lessons.title: Reading option quotes
objectives: Trade using bid, ask, and realistic mid prices

sections.heading: Bid, ask, last, mark
sections.body: Bid is the best price to sell; ask is the best price to buy. Last is the most recent trade. Mark is often the midpoint reference. Buyers usually pay near the ask; sellers receive near the bid.

sections.heading: Spreads and liquidity
sections.body: Tight bid/ask spreads (for example $0.01–$0.05 on liquid names) indicate better fills. Wide spreads mean hidden cost.

sections.heading: Symbol format
sections.body: Modern OCC symbols encode root, expiration (YYMMDD), call/put flag, and strike (8 digits with three implied decimals).

key_points: Never assume you can trade at last price
lessons.practice: Compare bid/ask width on your symbol's at-the-money call versus an out-of-the-money call.

lessons.title: Volume and open interest
objectives: Distinguish today's activity from outstanding contracts

sections.heading: Day volume
sections.body: Contracts traded today on that strike/expiry. High volume with rising open interest often suggests new positioning.

sections.heading: Open interest
sections.body: Contracts still open—not yet closed, exercised, or expired. Higher OI usually means better liquidity.

sections.heading: Unusual activity
sections.body: When day volume exceeds roughly twice open interest, investigate whether large players are entering before an event.

key_points: OI up + volume up: new positions. OI down + volume up: closures
lessons.practice: Pick one chain row and note volume, OI, and spread together.

lessons.title: Option order language
objectives: Open and close positions with correct instructions

sections.heading: Four core actions
sections.body: Buy to open (start long option), sell to open (start short option), buy to close (exit short), sell to close (exit long).

sections.heading: Market makers
sections.body: Market makers provide liquidity by quoting bid and ask. They earn the spread and help you trade when no natural counterparty is available.

key_points: Closing language matters—do not sell to open when you mean sell to close
lessons.practice: State aloud whether your next paper trade is opening or closing.

lessons.title: American vs European exercise
objectives: Pick valuation model and strategy with exercise style in mind

sections.heading: European
sections.body: Exercise only at expiration. Common in index options settled for cash (no share delivery).

sections.heading: American
sections.body: Exercise allowed before expiration. Most U.S. listed equity options are American-style. Early exercise matters for deep ITM puts, dividends, and short calls.

key_points: Use American-style modeling for U.S. equity options when early exercise is plausible
lessons.practice: Toggle European vs American in the Options P&L simulator and compare deep ITM put values.

lessons.title: Intrinsic and time value
objectives: Decompose premium into obvious and conditional components

sections.heading: Intrinsic value
sections.body: For calls: max(stock − strike, 0). For puts: max(strike − stock, 0). This is immediate exercise value at expiration.

sections.heading: Time value
sections.body: Premium minus intrinsic value. It reflects time, volatility, and interest/dividend carry. It decays toward zero at expiration.

key_points: At expiration, only intrinsic value remains
lessons.practice: Set simulation mode to expiration and move price across the strike.

lessons.title: Implied volatility and premium
objectives: Understand why correct direction can still lose money

sections.heading: What IV represents
sections.body: Implied volatility is the market's embedded expectation of future movement. Higher IV means more expensive options.

sections.heading: IV crush
sections.body: After events (earnings, FDA, macro shocks), IV often falls. Long options can lose value even if price barely moves.

sections.heading: Relative IV
sections.body: Judge IV against its own history (percentile) and versus realized volatility—not as a single absolute number.

key_points: High IV favors defined-risk premium selling; low IV favors buying convexity
lessons.practice: Run a scenario with +0 price move and −10 vol points in the simulator.

lessons.title: Greeks overview
objectives: Interpret delta, gamma, theta, vega, and rho at a practical level

sections.heading: Delta
sections.body: Approximate change in option price for a $1 move in the stock. Calls: 0 to +1. Puts: 0 to −1.

sections.heading: Gamma
sections.body: How fast delta changes when the stock moves. Highest near at-the-money close to expiration.

sections.heading: Theta
sections.body: Daily time decay, all else equal. Long options usually lose theta; short options usually collect it with tail risk.

sections.heading: Vega and rho
sections.body: Vega: sensitivity to a 1-point IV change. Rho: sensitivity to interest rates—more relevant for long-dated options.

key_points: Greeks change constantly—treat them as estimates
lessons.practice: Review the Greek metrics under the Options P&L simulator after changing IV and days elapsed.

lessons.title: Choosing ITM, ATM, or OTM
objectives: Match strike to goal: hedge, income, or speculation

sections.heading: Decision guide
sections.body: Hedging: often ITM puts or calls for higher delta. Income: ATM or OTM short options where theta is efficient. Speculation with small capital: OTM with lower probability. Strong directional view with defined risk: ATM or slight OTM spreads.

sections.heading: ROI thinking
sections.body: Compare expected return on capital to probability of success. Higher delta options cost more but behave more like stock.

key_points: There is no single best strike—only best fit for the plan
lessons.practice: Model three strikes on the same expiry in the single-leg simulator.

lessons.title: Rates and dividends
objectives: See how carry factors nudge call and put values

sections.heading: Interest rates
sections.body: Higher rates tend to increase call values and decrease put values slightly because of the present value of the strike.

sections.heading: Dividends
sections.body: Expected dividends reduce call values and increase put values because the stock is expected to drop on the ex-dividend date.

key_points: Dividend dates matter for short calls and deep ITM American options
lessons.practice: Adjust dividend yield in the simulator and note call vs put sensitivity.

lessons.title: Market regime overview
objectives: Start with environment, not strategy name

sections.heading: Three regimes
sections.body: Risk-on: volatility often falls, growth leads, dips get bought. Neutral/defensive: chop, elevated IV, earnings sold. Risk-off: correlations rise, IV spikes, capital preservation first.

sections.heading: Macro vs flow
sections.body: Macro sets the backdrop (rates, growth, policy). Flow is how money actually moves—what you trade against.

key_points: The market pays for adapting to context, not for having an opinion
lessons.practice: Label today's session as risk-on, neutral, or risk-off with one reason.

lessons.title: Volatility regimes
objectives: Link VIX direction to strategy families

sections.heading: VIX as thermometer
sections.body: Falling VIX often supports risk-on behavior. Stable mid-range VIX suits income structures. Rising VIX favors protection and smaller size.

sections.heading: High vs low IV on the stock
sections.body: High IV: favor defined-risk credit structures if you expect stability. Low IV: favor buying options or spreads for convexity.

key_points: Do not buy expensive options without a catalyst for movement
lessons.practice: Open Market scenario lab and pick rules matching today's regime.

lessons.title: Classifying implied volatility
objectives: Judge IV relative to history and the underlying

sections.heading: Rough scale (equity context)
sections.body: Below ~25% can be low for many large caps. 25–45% is common. Above ~45–50% is elevated. Above ~70% is extreme/event-driven. Always compare to the symbol's own history.

sections.heading: IV vs realized
sections.body: IV above realized volatility by several points: options expensive. IV below realized: options relatively cheap.

key_points: Sector matters—tech and biotech run higher than utilities
lessons.practice: Note your symbol's IV % in the strategy lab and classify it low/medium/high.

lessons.title: If this, then that
objectives: Map conditions to stock + option structures

sections.heading: Risk-on
sections.body: Favor stock, call spreads, long calls, momentum entries. Avoid aggressive premium selling that caps upside too early.

sections.heading: Neutral + high IV
sections.body: Favor covered calls, put credit spreads, iron condors, diagonals—structures that earn theta with defined risk.

sections.heading: Risk-off
sections.body: Reduce size, hold cash, buy puts, use collars, avoid heroics. Survival beats brilliance.

key_points: Structure beats direction when the market is uncertain
lessons.practice: Complete the pre-trade checklist before your next options trade.

lessons.title: Stock vs long call
objectives: Compare linear stock risk to leveraged option risk

sections.heading: Long stock
sections.body: Full upside and downside per share. Capital intensive. No expiration.

sections.heading: Long call
sections.body: Smaller upfront cost, maximum loss usually limited to premium, but requires direction, timing, and often favorable IV.

key_points: Calls are not 'cheap stock'—they are a bet on path and time
lessons.practice: Compare stock simulator P&L vs call simulator P&L for the same % move.

lessons.title: Protective put
objectives: Insure a stock position with defined downside

sections.heading: Structure
sections.body: Own shares plus buy a put. You keep upside minus premium; downside is cushioned below the strike.

sections.heading: When it fits
sections.body: Before earnings, during macro stress, or when you want to hold shares but fear a near-term drawdown.

key_points: Insurance has a cost—break-even moves up by the premium paid
lessons.practice: Load the protective put template in Strategy payoff lab.

lessons.title: Covered call
objectives: Generate income on stock you are willing to sell higher

sections.heading: Structure
sections.body: Own at least 100 shares per contract and sell a call against them. Collect premium; cap upside at strike plus premium.

sections.heading: When it fits
sections.body: Neutral to mildly bullish view, medium/high IV, willingness to sell shares at the strike.

key_points: Does not remove downside risk on the stock—only partially offsets with premium
lessons.practice: Try covered call template; move price down and up in the scenario slider.

lessons.title: Cash-secured put
objectives: Get paid to wait for a lower entry price

sections.heading: Structure
sections.body: Sell a put and reserve cash to buy stock if assigned. Keep premium if stock stays above strike.

sections.heading: Risk
sections.body: If stock falls far below strike, you buy at an effective price of strike minus premium—but still face further losses if shares keep dropping.

key_points: Only sell puts on names you want to own at the strike
lessons.practice: Model assignment scenarios in Strategy payoff lab with Custom legs.

lessons.title: Vertical credit spreads
objectives: Earn premium with capped risk

sections.heading: Bull put spread
sections.body: Sell put at higher strike, buy put at lower strike. Bullish to neutral. Max gain is net credit; max loss is width minus credit.

sections.heading: Bear call spread
sections.body: Sell call at lower strike, buy call at higher strike. Bearish to neutral. Same credit-spread mechanics.

key_points: Close winners before expiration—do not need max profit to be successful
lessons.practice: Load bull call spread and bear put spread templates and compare payoff shapes.

lessons.title: Iron condor
objectives: Profit from range-bound prices with defined risk

sections.heading: Structure
sections.body: Combine bull put spread below the market and bear call spread above. Profit if price finishes between short strikes.

sections.heading: When it fits
sections.body: Low expected movement, elevated IV, neutral outlook. Watch gap risk through the range.

key_points: Max loss occurs outside the long strikes—know that dollar amount before entry
lessons.practice: Use iron butterfly / iron condor templates and test prices outside the range.

lessons.title: Straddle and strangle
objectives: Trade expected large moves without picking direction

sections.heading: Long straddle
sections.body: Buy call and put at same strike. Needs a large move to overcome double premium and theta.

sections.heading: Long strangle
sections.body: Buy OTM call and OTM put. Cheaper but needs an even larger move.

key_points: Best when IV is relatively low before a known catalyst
lessons.practice: Long straddle template with before-expiration Greek mode.

lessons.title: Collar
objectives: Protect stock while financing part of the put with a short call

sections.heading: Structure
sections.body: Long stock, long put, short call. Creates a band of outcomes between put floor and call ceiling.

sections.heading: When it fits
sections.body: After a large gain, into an uncertain period, or when you want defined risk without selling shares.

key_points: Net cost depends on put vs call premium—can be near zero cost
lessons.practice: Collar template in Strategy payoff lab.

lessons.title: Diagonal call spread
objectives: Finance long-dated exposure by selling short-dated calls

sections.heading: Structure
sections.body: Buy longer-dated call (lower strike or same), sell shorter-dated call nearer the money. Collect theta on the short leg while keeping convexity on the long leg.

sections.heading: Management
sections.body: If price is flat: let short call decay and resell. If price rips: close short leg first, let long run. If price drops: decide whether thesis is intact before reselling calls.

key_points: Short leg may require margin—check broker requirements
lessons.practice: Custom legs: long call 90 DTE, short call 30 DTE; test three price paths.

lessons.title: Stock plus bull call spread
objectives: Combine stock anchor with defined-risk option leverage

sections.heading: Structure
sections.body: Own shares for core delta. Add bull call spread (buy ITM or ATM call, sell OTM call) for additional upside with capped option risk.

sections.heading: Management
sections.body: If price rallies hard, consider closing spread at 80–90% of max value, keeping stock, then selling covered calls higher.

key_points: Stock provides patience; spread provides efficiency
lessons.practice: Build stock + two call legs in Custom strategy table.

lessons.title: LEAPS with short call
objectives: Stock substitute with income overlay

sections.heading: Structure
sections.body: Buy long-dated call (LEAPS) instead of all cash stock. Periodically sell short-dated calls against it (diagonal/calendar style).

sections.heading: When it fits
sections.body: Bullish long-term view but want lower capital tie-up and willing to manage short calls.

key_points: LEAPS still suffer from IV and time if thesis delays
lessons.practice: Compare LEAPS debit vs stock purchase in a spreadsheet using simulator premiums.

lessons.title: Rolling covered calls
objectives: Adjust strikes and time when price approaches short call

sections.heading: Roll up
sections.body: Close current short call and sell higher strike, same expiry—recover upside when stock rises.

sections.heading: Roll out
sections.body: Same strike, later expiry—collect more premium when price is sticky near strike.

sections.heading: When not to roll
sections.body: If assignment at strike is acceptable or rolling costs erase edge, let shares be called away.

key_points: Roll only if math improves expected outcome—not from fear alone
lessons.practice: Paper-trade a roll when stock crosses 90% of your short strike.

lessons.title: Managing diagonals
objectives: Protect the long leg; treat the short leg as disposable on squeezes

sections.heading: Flat market
sections.body: Let short option decay; resell after expiration if thesis intact.

sections.heading: Strong rally
sections.body: Close short call quickly; optional: sell far OTM call only if IV is extreme.

sections.heading: Decline
sections.body: Let short expire worthless if possible; reassess long call or sell new lower call only if still bullish.

key_points: Never defend the short leg by sacrificing the long leg
lessons.practice: List your action for each of three scenarios before entering a diagonal.

lessons.title: Closing spreads at a profit
objectives: Bank gains without needing maximum theoretical value

sections.heading: Credit spreads
sections.body: Many traders close at 50–80% of max profit to reduce gamma risk into expiration.

sections.heading: How to close
sections.body: Use a single combo order (buy back short, sell long) when possible for cleaner fills.

key_points: Close the entire spread—do not leave one naked leg
lessons.practice: Identify max profit on your spread and set a profit-taking level at 70%.

lessons.title: Margin on short options
objectives: Understand why short legs tie up buying power

sections.heading: Naked short options
sections.body: Highest margin—avoid unless intentional and capitalized.

sections.heading: Spreads and diagonals
sections.body: Defined-risk spreads often use less margin than naked shorts. Diagonals may still reserve margin on the short leg—verify with broker.

sections.heading: Covered call
sections.body: Stock ownership covers the call—no additional short-call margin if fully covered.

key_points: Check margin impact before entry, not after a squeeze
lessons.practice: Note which legs in your strategy table are short options.

lessons.title: Pre-trade questions
objectives: Force discipline before capital is at risk

sections.heading: Checklist
sections.body: What is the regime? Is IV cheap or expensive? What is my max loss? What proves me wrong? What happens if price does nothing? Does this match my time horizon?

key_points: If you cannot answer clearly, wait
lessons.practice: Use the Pre-trade checklist page before every new options structure.

strategy_playbook.name: Long call
strategy_playbook.when_to_use: Moderate upside view, willing to risk full premium, catalyst within the option's life.
strategy_playbook.risks: Time decay and IV drop can hurt even if direction is right.

strategy_playbook.name: Bull call spread
strategy_playbook.when_to_use: Defined-risk bullish bet with lower cost than naked call.

strategy_playbook.name: Covered call
strategy_playbook.when_to_use: Income on shares you own; okay selling at strike.
strategy_playbook.risks: Stock can fall more than premium collected.

strategy_playbook.name: Cash-secured put
strategy_playbook.when_to_use: Want to buy stock lower and earn premium while waiting.

strategy_playbook.name: Long put
strategy_playbook.when_to_use: Downside view with limited premium risk.
strategy_playbook.risks: Timing and IV crush after events.

strategy_playbook.name: Iron condor
strategy_playbook.structure: Bull put spread + bear call spread
strategy_playbook.when_to_use: Expect price to stay in a range; IV elevated.

strategy_playbook.name: Long straddle
strategy_playbook.structure: Buy call and put same strike
strategy_playbook.when_to_use: Binary or large move expected, direction unclear.

strategy_playbook.name: Protective put
strategy_playbook.when_to_use: Hold shares but limit near-term downside.

strategy_playbook.name: Collar
strategy_playbook.structure: Long stock, long put, short call
strategy_playbook.when_to_use: Define a outcome band after gains or into uncertainty.

checklists.title: Daily regime check
items: Is VIX rising, falling, or stable?
Are more stocks advancing than declining?
Are bad headlines ignored or punished?
Is my symbol's IV above or below its recent average?

checklists.title: Pre-trade options checklist
items: What regime am I in (risk-on, neutral, risk-off)?
Is IV cheap, fair, or expensive for this symbol?
What is my maximum loss in dollars?
What price or date proves me wrong?
What happens if the stock does not move?
Does expiration match my catalyst timeline?
Have I modeled the trade in the payoff simulator?

checklists.title: Covered call management
items: Is IV still high enough to justify a new sale?
If price exceeds strike, will I roll, accept assignment, or close?
Did I calculate roll credit/debit before acting?
